pages.title: Services
pages.content:
Services

Services

Company audit, charity audit and examination, and grant assurance, each with its own engagement letter and fee.

pages.title: Company audit
pages.content:
Services

Company audit

Statutory audit for owner-managed companies and groups, signed by a partner who has met you.

Scope

When an audit is required

A statutory audit is required when a company crosses the size threshold set in company law. We do not print that threshold as a pound figure on this page. It moves when the law moves, and a copied number is how firms give the wrong answer. On the planning call we look at the latest accounts and say whether an audit is required or still a choice.

Many of our company clients come in the year they cross. Fenwick Joinery Ltd is that situation: a family joiner, a first statutory audit, timber stock that had to be counted properly. Others ask for an audit before they must, because a bank, a buyer or a new shareholder wants one. We will do a voluntary audit on the same process. We will not dress a lighter review up as an audit.

The published company fee, £6,500 ex VAT, covers a statutory audit where turnover is up to £15 million. Above that, we agree a fee in the engagement letter before any work starts. We would rather turn the work away than invent a day rate at the end.

Scope

What we test

Three things decide most owner-managed audits. We test all three, and we say so at the start.

Statutory audit

Company audit from £6,500

Group audit

Parent and up to 3 subsidiaries, from £11,800

Stock count attendance

Per site, per day, from £780

Engagement

Stock, revenue and the rest

Stock. We attend the count where stock is material. We check that the sheets match the aisle, that goods received and goods sent around the year-end are in the right period, and that the final listing agrees to what was counted. Attendance is charged at £780 per site, per day, on top of the audit fee.

Revenue. We sample sales through the year, including the invoices and the ledger, and we look hard at the weeks either side of the year-end. Owner-managed businesses often have a handful of customers that make up most of the turnover. Those customers get more of our time, not less.

The consolidation, where there is a group. Tomasz Wierzbicki leads group work. The published group fee is £11,800 ex VAT for a parent and up to three subsidiaries. Calloway Freight Group was that shape: three subsidiaries, and a first consolidation.

A joinery workshop in the year-end week: the stock is counted where it stands.

Engagement

What the management letter contains

The management letter is the note that travels with the signed opinion. It is not a second audit report, and it is not a list of every test we performed.

It sets out the points we think the directors should deal with before the next year-end. On a first audit that is often the count itself: how sheets are controlled, who stops the warehouse, how obsolete stock is identified. It also records adjustments we proposed and whether you booked them, and any place where the records made the audit slower than the timetable.

You see the letter in draft at the findings meeting, which sits in fieldwork between week 4 and week 9. The partner who will sign is in that meeting. The letter is issued with the opinion, by week 12, when records were with us by week 4. It is written in plain sentences. We do not use it to sell you extra work.

Fees

Company fees, as published

Three lines from the firm-wide fee list apply most often to company work. All figures are in pounds sterling, ex VAT, and they are from figures. The number in your engagement letter is the number you pay.

Company statutory audit (turnover up to £15m)

For an owner-managed company with turnover up to £15m.

from £6,500

Group audit, parent + up to 3 subsidiaries

A parent and up to 3 subsidiaries, including a first consolidation.

from £11,800

Stock count attendance (per site, per day)

Any day by arrangement, including weekends.

from £780

All fees ex VAT, fixed in the engagement letter.

Scope

What if we have more than three subsidiaries?

The published group fee stops at a parent and three subsidiaries. It is £11,800 ex VAT. A further company is not folded into that figure quietly. Before we are appointed we tell you whether we can take the group and what the fee in the engagement letter would be. We do not publish a tariff beyond the seven lines on the fees page, and we do not start fieldwork while that conversation is still open.

If a company looks dormant and you are unsure it counts, bring the latest accounts to the planning call. Thirty minutes is enough to see the shape of the group. We reply within 2 working days if you write first. The call itself is free. Tomasz Wierzbicki is the partner who would sign a group opinion, and he is the partner who should be on that call.

pages.title: Charity audit and independent examination
pages.content:
Services

Charity audit and independent examination

An examination or an audit for grant-funded charities, with restricted funds read as part of the same file.

Scope

Examination or audit

Charity law draws a line by income. Under the line, an independent examination is the report most charities need. Over the line, a statutory audit is required. We are not going to type the pound figure for that line onto this page. The line is set outside this firm, and it changes. Using an old number is how a treasurer commissions the wrong report.

What we will do, on a free 30-minute planning call, is read the latest accounts and tell you which report you need this year. If you are near the line, we say so. Riverside Food Larder came to us for an examination and later needed an audit. The same partner, Helen Osei, stayed with them across that change. You should not have to retell the charity to a new firm in the year the income grows.

An examination is not a light audit, and an audit is not a heavier examination with a different cover. The testing and the signature follow the regime that actually applies. We will not offer the cheaper report if the law requires the other one.

Scope

Restricted funds

Restricted funds are the usual hard part of a charity engagement. A grant that may only be spent on a stated purpose has to be shown that way, and the spending has to be traced to that purpose. We test that trail. We do not redesign your fund structure, and we do not advise you to rewrite a donor's condition so that the accounts look simpler.

Independent examination

For charities under the audit line, from £1,450

Statutory audit

For charities over the line, from £4,800

Grant assurance

A report per funder, from £1,900

Engagement

How restricted funds are tested

If you have more than one funder, each with its own wording, bring the grant letters to planning. Grace Mbeki leads grants work and will say which letters the examination or the audit must cover. A separate grant assurance report, where a funder asks for one, is a different engagement at £1,900 per funder, ex VAT. It is not hidden inside the examination fee or the audit fee.

The examination fee starts at £1,450 ex VAT. The charity statutory audit starts at £4,800 ex VAT. Both are from figures, fixed in the engagement letter. Both follow the same payment split: 40 percent at planning, 60 percent on signing.

Engagement

The trustees' report

We read the trustees' report against the accounts. Numbers in the narrative that do not match the accounts are raised before anything is signed, not in a footnote afterwards. Restricted fund descriptions must match the movements in the fund notes. If the report describes an activity the accounts do not show, we ask you to change one or the other.

Helen Osei reviews that reading on charity engagements. The findings meeting, in weeks 4 to 9 after the year-end, is where trustees see the points in draft. We would rather a trustee disagree with us then, while the report can still be corrected.

The timetable is the firm's usual one. Records with us by week 4, opinion signed within 12 weeks of the year-end. A partner signs. On a charity, that partner is Helen Osei unless the engagement letter names otherwise. The management letter that accompanies the opinion is written for the trustees, in the same plain language as the report they will publish.

Fees

Charity fees, as published

Two lines from the firm-wide fee list apply to charities. Both are ex VAT and both are starting figures: the fee you pay is the one in the engagement letter.

Charity independent examination

For a charity that needs an examination rather than an audit.

from £1,450

Charity statutory audit

For a charity over the audit threshold, with restricted funds and the trustees’ report.

from £4,800

All fees ex VAT, fixed in the engagement letter.

Scope

Is an independent examination enough for our funder?

Sometimes the law allows an examination and a funder still asks for an audit, or for a report in the funder's own format. Those are different requests. We will tell you which ones you actually have.

If the funder has specified a report, that is grant assurance, priced at £1,900 per funder, ex VAT, and timed against the claim. If the charity is over the statutory line, the examination is the wrong product and we will say that before you appoint us. If the charity is under the line and the funder has not asked for anything further, the examination at £1,450 ex VAT is the engagement we propose.

Bring the grant letter and the latest accounts to the planning call. We reply within 2 working days. The call is 30 minutes and free. Helen Osei takes charity appointments. Northgate Youth Music Trust is the sort of case where the charity report and the funder reports had to be told apart before anyone was appointed.

pages.title: Grant assurance
pages.content:
Services

Grant assurance

Reports a funder has specified, timed so the claim and the year-end are not two arguments.

Scope

Reports a funder has specified

Some grants ask for more than the charity's examination or audit. The funder names the figures it wants tested, the period, and the form of the report. We do that work as its own engagement. We do not tuck it into the audit and hope the funder accepts the opinion instead.

Northgate Youth Music Trust needed two such reports, both aligned to one year-end. That is the shape we prefer. One set of records, two reports that a trustee can reconcile to the same accounts. Grace Mbeki leads the grant work. Helen Osei signs charity opinions. Where the funder requires a named report rather than an opinion, the engagement letter says which partner is responsible for that report.

We read the grant conditions before we accept. If a condition asks us to certify something we cannot see, we say so at the planning call and we do not take that part of the work.

Engagement

Agreed-upon procedures

Agreed-upon procedures means we do the tests the funder has listed, and we report what those tests showed. We do not widen them into an audit, and we do not narrow them because a test is awkward. The list is agreed in the engagement letter before we start. If the funder changes the list after the letter, we pause and agree the change in writing.

The procedures usually follow the money: whether the grant was received, whether it was spent on the purpose named, and whether the invoices support that spend. Where the funder also asks about goods, we attend if attendance is the only honest way to answer. Stock count attendance remains £780 per site, per day, ex VAT, and only if a count is actually required.

You receive the factual findings. We do not say that a funder will release the next instalment. The report says what we were asked to check and what we found.

Engagement

Timing the work to the claim

Grant claims rarely fall on the same day as a filing date. We build the grant timetable from the claim date backwards, and we put that date in the engagement letter.

Where the charity also has a year-end audit or examination, we align the two. Fieldwork for the statutory work runs in weeks 4 to 9, and the opinion is signed within 12 weeks of the year-end when records arrive by week 4. The funder report is planned against the claim, not against a vague promise to do it after the audit. On Northgate Youth Music Trust both funder reports were set to the same year-end so the trust was not preparing two closings.

If the claim date cannot be met honestly, we tell you at planning. A 30-minute call is enough to compare the claim date with the state of the records. We reply within 2 working days. The call is free.

Fees

The fee for each funder

A grant assurance report is £1,900 ex VAT per funder. Two funders are two reports. We do not blend them into a single unpublished price. Each letter states the procedures for that funder and the fee for that report.

Grant assurance report (per funder)

One report per funder, timed to the grant claim and the year-end.

from £1,900

All fees ex VAT, fixed in the engagement letter.

Contact

Talk to the grants team

The figure is a from price. It is fixed in the engagement letter once we have read the funder's instructions. Payment is 40 percent at planning and 60 percent when the report is signed. VAT is extra. A charity statutory audit at £4,800, or an examination at £1,450, is a separate line if you need one as well.

Nothing in the fee means the funder will accept the claim. You are paying for the procedures, the attendance we have agreed, and a partner who will put a name to the report.

Book a planning call or email hello@akira-audit.example. We reply within 2 working days.

pages.title: How an audit runs
pages.content:
Engagement

How an audit runs

One path from the engagement letter to a partner’s signature, with every date counted from the year-end.

Stage 1

Appointment, two weeks before the year-end

Appointment is the engagement letter. We aim to have it signed two weeks before the year-end, so the count and the sample are planned rather than improvised.

The letter names the client, the year, the report you have asked for, and the partner who will sign. It states the fee, ex VAT, and the split: 40 percent at planning, 60 percent on signing. It also states the two rules. We attend every material stock count, and a partner signs the opinion personally.

You will have had the planning call before this letter. That call is 30 minutes and free. If we cannot see how an opinion could be reached, the letter is where we stop, not where we hope for the best. Akira Bennett, Helen Osei or Tomasz Wierzbicki is the partner named, according to whether the work is a company, a charity or a group.

Stage 2

Planning, the risk meeting and the document list

Planning is a risk meeting and a document list. We sit down with the person who keeps the records, and we agree where this year is likely to go wrong. For a joiner that is often timber. For a food larder it is restricted funds. For a group it is the first consolidation.

The document list is short on purpose. We ask for what the testing will actually use, not for a copy of the entire filing room. You know from the list what to have ready by week 4. Records that arrive by week 4 are what the later timetable depends on.

Priya Raman, audit manager, runs this stage day to day and stays with the engagement through to the findings meeting. The partner comes to the risk meeting. We do not hand you a list written by someone who will never see the file.

Stage 3

Observation at the year-end count

If stock is material, we attend the count at the year-end. This is the stage we will not skip. Lucas Ferreira leads stock and inventory. The fee for attendance is £780 per site, per day, ex VAT, and it is quoted in the letter rather than added afterwards.

We agree the day, including a Saturday or a Sunday if that is when your warehouse actually stops. Office hours at Wapping Quay Studios are Monday to Friday, 08:30 to 17:30, and the office is closed at the weekend. The count is the exception. We come any day by arrangement.

On the day we watch the count, we test a sample of lines ourselves, and we take a note of goods moving in and out. We do not take over your count. Your staff still count. We are there to see that the count you rely on is the count that happened.

Stage 4

Testing and findings, weeks 4 to 9

Fieldwork runs in weeks 4 to 9 after the year-end, provided the records were with us by week 4. We test the areas named at planning. Revenue, stock listings, grant spending and, for a group, the subsidiary returns are the usual core.

You do not wait until the end for bad news. As a point becomes clear, we raise it. The findings meeting sits inside this window. We go through the points on the page with your finance lead, and the partner who will sign is there. Adjustments are agreed or left disagreed in that room.

The management letter is drafted from that meeting. It lists what the directors or trustees should change before next year, and what we proposed you book this year. It is still a draft at this stage. The opinion has not been signed.

Stage 5

Signed opinion, by week 12

A partner signs the opinion, and the management letter is issued with it. The timetable we work to is a signature within 12 weeks of the year-end, when records arrived by week 4. The partner named in the engagement letter is the partner who signs. That duty is not passed to a manager.

Signing is also the moment the remaining fee falls due: 60 percent, ex VAT, against the figure in the letter. The first 40 percent was billed at planning.

If the records cannot support an opinion by week 12, we do not sign one to protect the date. We tell you what is missing and what that does to the timetable. The 12 weeks are a plan we will keep when the records allow it. The form of the opinion follows those records.

Scope

What should we prepare?

The list below is what we ask you to prepare. It is the same list for a company and a charity, with extra lines where they apply.

Have the engagement letter signed two weeks before the year-end.

Send the documents on the planning list so they are with us by week 4.

Name a person who can walk the count with us, if stock is material, and make sure the warehouse can actually stop.

Keep invoices and the sales record ready for the samples we pick in weeks 4 to 9.

Have draft accounts before the findings meeting, so we are reviewing your numbers and not building them.

Charities also bring the restricted fund analysis and the draft trustees' report. Groups bring the returns for the parent and for up to three subsidiaries. Grant clients bring the funder's instructions and the claim date. We do not ask for a data room, and we do not add documents in the last week that were never on the list.

pages.title: Cases
pages.content:
Case

Cases

Four engagements told plainly, with qualitative outcomes and the timings that were met.

Case 1

Fenwick Joinery Ltd

Fenwick Joinery Ltd is a family joinery business. The year they appointed us was the year they crossed the statutory audit threshold. It was their first statutory audit, and the stock that mattered was timber.

We attended the timber count, because a material count is one we go to in person. Their staff counted the boards and the finished doors. We tested a sample of lines and we noted goods moving around the year-end. Revenue was tested from the invoices and the ledger, with more time on the customers that made up most of the turnover. Akira Bennett leads company work of this kind, and a partner signed the opinion.

The outcome was a completed first audit and a management letter the directors could use the next year. Records were in by week 4, and the opinion was signed within 12 weeks of the year-end. We do not publish a stock adjustment or a percentage. The letter said what the count showed. The opinion said what the partner could sign.

Case 2

Riverside Food Larder

Riverside Food Larder is a grant-funded charity. The difficult part was restricted funds: money given for stated purposes, which had to be spent and shown that way. They began with an independent examination. A later year took them over the line, and the examination became a statutory audit.

Helen Osei led the charity work across that change, so the larder did not start again with a new firm in the year the report changed. We traced restricted income and spending, and we read the trustees' report against the fund notes. Where the narrative and the accounts disagreed, the findings meeting was used to put one of them right before anything was signed.

The outcome was continuity, not a new claim about fundraising. The charity kept a firm that had already examined the funds and could then audit them. Examination starts at £1,450 and the charity audit at £4,800, ex VAT. The audit year was signed on the 12-week timetable once records were in by week 4.

Case 3

Calloway Freight Group

Calloway Freight Group appointed us for a first consolidation. The group was a parent and three subsidiaries, which is the shape our published group fee describes. Tomasz Wierzbicki led the engagement.

The difficulty was doing a consolidation for the first time: three sets of numbers, balances between the companies, and a parent that had not had to show the group before. We agreed the subsidiary returns at planning, tested them in the fieldwork window of weeks 4 to 9, and took the consolidation adjustments through the findings meeting with the finance lead.

The outcome was a first group audit, signed by the partner, with a management letter that listed what the next consolidation needed from each company. The fee for this shape of group starts at £11,800 ex VAT. We do not decorate the opinion with adjectives. It was the opinion the records supported, signed within 12 weeks of the year-end because the returns arrived by week 4.

Case 4

Northgate Youth Music Trust

Northgate Youth Music Trust needed two reports that funders had specified. The useful decision, made at appointment, was to align both reports to one year-end rather than run two closings.

Grace Mbeki led the grant work. The procedures were the ones each funder had written down. They were agreed in the engagement letter and not quietly widened into an audit. Where the trust also needed its charity accounts reported on, that remained a separate examination or audit under Helen Osei, with its own fee. Each funder report was priced at the published figure of £1,900 ex VAT.

The outcome was two reports a trustee could tie back to the same year, prepared against the claim dates those funders had set. We do not say the claims were paid. Payment of a grant is the funder's decision. Our part ended when the agreed procedures had been reported and a partner had put a name to each report.

pages.title: Fees
pages.content:
Fees

Fees

Seven published fees in pounds sterling, ex VAT, fixed in the engagement letter before work starts.

Fees

From figure to fixed fee

Every line is in pounds sterling and every line is ex VAT. Every line is a from figure. The engagement letter replaces from with a fixed fee before we start. If the work is larger than the line describes, turnover above £15 million, a further subsidiary, or a funder whose instructions sit far outside a standard report, we agree the fixed fee in that letter or we decline. We do not keep a second price list.

Scope

What the fee covers

The fee in the letter covers the stages named for that engagement. Appointment, with the letter signed about two weeks before the year-end. Planning, including the risk meeting and the document list. Fieldwork in weeks 4 to 9. A findings meeting. A partner's signature and the management letter, aimed at week 12 when records arrived by week 4.

It covers the partner's time to sign and the partner's time to refuse to sign. You are not billed a success fee for an unmodified opinion, and you are not billed extra because the opinion had to be reserved. The 40 percent and the 60 percent are shares of the same fixed fee.

Stock count attendance is not silently included. Where a count is material it is quoted at £780 per site, per day. A grant report is not silently included in a charity audit. It is £1,900 for that funder. A readiness review before the first audit year is the separate £950 line.

Engagement

What changes a fee

The starting figure changes, before the letter is signed, when the work sits outside the line that figure describes.

Turnover above £15 million is outside the company fee. A subsidiary beyond the third is outside the group fee. A second funder is a second grant report, not a free annex to the first. A second stock location, or a second day at the same location, is another £780. A charity that has moved from examination to audit moves from the £1,450 line to the £4,800 line. That is a different report, not a surcharge on the old one.

We also re-price, in the letter and not afterwards, when the records described at planning are not the records we find. If a single company is in fact a group, we stop and rewrite the letter. The planning call, 30 minutes and free, is where most of these points come out. We reply within 2 working days if you send the accounts first.

Fees

How you pay

Payment is 40 percent at planning and 60 percent when the partner signs. Both parts are invoiced in pounds sterling, ex VAT. The fee itself does not move between those two invoices. If the letter says £6,500, planning is 40 percent of that £6,500 and signing is the rest.

We do not take the fee as a share of any adjustment, and we do not hold an opinion against an invoice that has nothing to do with it. The 60 percent is due when we sign, because that is the work the letter described. If we cannot sign, we tell you why, and we deal with the fee in that same conversation rather than by a clause you never saw.

A pre-audit readiness review is billed on the same split. So is a grant report, and so is a stock-count day that has its own letter. Sam Ellery, practice manager, answers billing questions in office hours.

Fees

Are these prices inclusive of VAT?

No. Every published fee is exclusive of VAT, and the engagement letter shows the fee the same way. We do not add a round sum to stand in for VAT, and we do not quote a fee that already has VAT folded in. The invoice shows the ex VAT fee and the VAT in the ordinary way.

The currency is pounds sterling on every engagement. We do not convert these figures for a client who keeps books in another currency. If your accounts are in another currency, we still bill in pounds, at the fee in the letter.

The split is unchanged by VAT. Forty percent is due at planning and 60 percent when the partner signs, calculated on the ex VAT fee, with VAT added to each invoice. Office hours for a question about an invoice are Monday to Friday, 08:30 to 17:30, on +44 117 000 0419 or hello@akira-audit.example.

pages.title: About
pages.content:
About

About

A Bristol audit firm opened in 2009 for the companies and charities larger practices decline.

2009

Engagement

Why the firm opened in 2009

Akira Bennett left a large firm in 2009 and set up Akira Audit LLP. The work she wanted was still there: family companies that had grown into an audit, and charities whose grants depended on a report a board could trust. Larger practices were declining that work. She opened a firm that would take it.

The office is still Wapping Quay Studios, 3 Gaol Ferry Steps, Bristol BS1, United Kingdom. There are 26 people and three partners. Akira Bennett leads company audits. Helen Osei leads charities. Tomasz Wierzbicki leads groups. Clients deal with the partner who will sign, not with a pool of staff they will never meet again.

We have not added offices in other cities. Stock counts are attended wherever the goods are, any day by arrangement. The rest of the year the work comes back to Bristol, and the opinion is signed here.

Scope

What independent means here

An audit is independent when the person who signs did not write the numbers, and when the report is made to the members or the trustees rather than to the director who wants a quieter year. That is the meaning we use.

We are appointed to look, to test, and to say what we found. We are not appointed to produce the result a board has already described to a funder or a bank. If the records cannot support an opinion, we say so before anyone pretends otherwise. The planning call exists for that conversation. It lasts 30 minutes and it is free. If we are the wrong firm, we would rather say that in the first half hour.

Independence also means a partner remains responsible after the fieldwork is finished. The team can do the testing. The name on the opinion is a partner's name, written by that partner.

Engagement

Two rules

We keep two rules, and we put them in the engagement letter so they are not a brochure line.

First, we attend every material stock count. A count that matters to the opinion is not left to a photograph or to a client's own sheet sent on afterwards. Lucas Ferreira leads stock and inventory work. Attendance is arranged for the year-end, including weekends when that is when you stop the warehouse. The published fee is £780 per site, per day, ex VAT.

Second, a partner signs every opinion personally. Akira Bennett, Helen Osei or Tomasz Wierzbicki signs. The signature is not delegated to a manager. Priya Raman runs the audit day to day as audit manager. She does not sign the opinion.

Both rules apply to companies, charities and grant reports. If we cannot attend a count that is material, or a partner cannot sign, we do not take the engagement.

Services

Three things you can hold us to

The three values on this page are the same two rules, plus the standard we use when they are tested.

We go to the count

If stock is material, a person from this firm is in the aisle with a count sheet, not briefed from a phone call the week after.

A partner signs

The opinion, and the management letter that goes with it, leave under a partner's name. You will have met that partner at appointment.

We will decline

Independent means we can refuse a timetable, a number, or a whole engagement. A free planning call is enough time to find out whether the work fits. We reply within 2 working days.

None of these is a promise about the kind of opinion you will receive. The opinion follows the records. The letter records attendance, a named partner, and a timetable: records by week 4, opinion signed within 12 weeks of year-end.

pages.title: People
pages.content:
People

People

Three partners who sign, and the managers and seniors who run the work beside them.

People

The three partners

Akira Bennett is the founding partner and leads company audits. She opened the firm in 2009 after leaving a large practice, so that owner-managed companies and charities would still have an auditor willing to take their work. She has led Akira Audit LLP since that year, and she signs company opinions herself.

Helen Osei is the partner for charities. She leads examinations and charity audits, and she reads the trustees' report against the accounts before anything is signed. Riverside Food Larder, and the charity side of Northgate Youth Music Trust, are the kind of engagements her name goes on.

Tomasz Wierzbicki is the partner for groups. He leads consolidations, including a parent with up to three subsidiaries. Calloway Freight Group, a first consolidation of three subsidiaries, is the kind of engagement he signs.

Only a partner signs an opinion. Which of the three signs is written in the engagement letter at appointment.

People

Who runs the work

Priya Raman is the audit manager. She runs the engagement from the document list through fieldwork and into the findings meeting in weeks 4 to 9. She does not sign the opinion. If you write to the firm during fieldwork, it is usually Priya who is in the file.

Lucas Ferreira is senior auditor for stock and inventory. He attends material stock counts, including counts arranged on a day the office itself is closed. Grace Mbeki is senior auditor for grants. She runs the agreed-upon procedures on funder reports and keeps those reports aligned to the claim date and to the year-end.

Sam Ellery is the practice manager. Appointments, invoices and the question of who can be at which site go through Sam. The phone is +44 117 000 0419 and the email is hello@akira-audit.example. Both are answered Monday to Friday, 08:30 to 17:30.

People

Qualifications, without a league table

Audit staff at the firm hold the ACA or the ACCA. We do not describe anyone here as a CTA, and this page is not an offer of tax advice. A qualification is how a person is allowed to do the work. It is not a ranking, and we do not print letters beside the seven names as if the letters were the reason to appoint us.

Akira Bennett has been here since the firm opened in 2009. The six colleagues named with her are introduced by the work they lead: charities, groups, the audit file, stock, grants, and the running of the practice. We do not add a joining year under each of those six. A year that does nothing for the opinion does not get printed for decoration.

The wider firm is 26 people. These seven are named because they are the ones a client meets. Extra hands in weeks 4 to 9 work under the named partner. They are not given a fresh profile for the length of one engagement.

pages.title: Contact
pages.content:
Contact

Contact

A free 30-minute planning call, a reply within 2 working days, and an office that keeps weekday hours.

Contact

How a planning call works

Email hello@akira-audit.example or call +44 117 000 0419 and ask for a planning call. Sam Ellery arranges it. We reply within 2 working days. The call is 30 minutes and it is free. It is a conversation, not a written proposal in disguise.

Send the latest accounts beforehand if you have them. In the half hour we say whether the work looks like a company audit, a charity examination, a charity audit, a group audit or a grant report, and which published fee line applies. If turnover is above £15 million, or there are more than three subsidiaries, we say that the published line does not cover you, and whether we can still be appointed.

The partner on the call is the partner who would sign. Akira Bennett for companies, Helen Osei for charities, Tomasz Wierzbicki for groups. If we are the wrong firm, we say so before a letter is drafted. If we can help, the letter is the next step, aimed at two weeks before your year-end.

Contact

Address, hours, phone and email

Address

Akira Audit LLP, Wapping Quay Studios, 3 Gaol Ferry Steps, Bristol BS1, United Kingdom

Hours

Mon–Fri 08:30–17:30

Phone

+44 117 000 0419

hello@akira-audit.example

The office is open Monday to Friday, 08:30 to 17:30. It is closed on Saturday and Sunday. Stock counts are the exception. We attend a material count on any day by arrangement, including the weekend if that is when the warehouse stops. Do not come to the studio on a Saturday expecting a meeting. Arrange the count, and arrange any meeting, while the office is open.

A visit is useful when you want to meet the partner before you appoint us. It is not required. Most planning calls are by phone. The address is for letters, for the signed engagement letter coming back, and for the few meetings that are better held in the room. The firm was opened here in 2009 and the office has not moved.

Contact

What should I send before we speak?

Send the latest signed accounts, if a year has already been filed. If you are a charity, add the latest trustees' report, and any grant letter that asks for a report of its own. If you are a group, add a list of the companies and which one owns which. If this may be the first year an audit is required, say that in the email. You do not need a stock listing or a full set of invoices before we have spoken.

Do not send passwords, and do not send anything you would not put in an ordinary email. The free call is there to decide whether we should be appointed. The document list comes after the engagement letter, and we ask for those records by week 4.

If you are writing about a count already fixed for this weekend, telephone +44 117 000 0419 in office hours. A count can be attended any day by arrangement, but the arrangement is made while the office is open, Monday to Friday, 08:30 to 17:30. We reply to written messages within 2 working days.

posts.title: Preparing for your first stock count
posts.excerpt: What to have ready when an auditor attends your year-end count for the first time, and what we will and will not do in the aisle.
posts.content:
The first statutory audit often arrives in the same year the warehouse has to be counted in front of someone from outside the company. You have crossed the threshold. The stock is material. Akira Audit LLP will not sign an opinion on that stock from a sheet emailed the week after. We attend every material stock count. This note is what to do before we arrive.

Start from the date of the count, which is your year-end, and work backwards. We want the engagement letter signed two weeks before that date. The letter names the partner who will sign the opinion, states the fee, and states that attendance at the count is part of the work. Akira Bennett leads company audits. Lucas Ferreira, senior auditor for stock and inventory, is the person most likely to be in the aisle with your staff. You should know both names before the day.

Your own staff still count. We do not take the boards out of their hands and run the count for you. We watch, we test lines ourselves, and we note goods coming in and goods going out. A count that stops the warehouse is a better count than one fitted around a busy dispatch. If the only day the warehouse can stop is a Saturday or a Sunday, say so. The office at Wapping Quay Studios, 3 Gaol Ferry Steps, Bristol BS1, is open Monday to Friday, 08:30 to 17:30, and closed at the weekend. The count is different: we attend on any day, by arrangement. Make that arrangement in office hours, by phone on +44 117 000 0419 or by email to hello@akira-audit.example.

Have ordinary things ready, not a performance. Know where the stock sits, including a second site if there is one, because attendance is charged per site, per day. Have people there who can tell finished work from scrap. Use count sheets that have not been completed in advance for the lines we will test. Keep a record of the last deliveries and the last dispatches, so sales and purchases around the year-end fall in the right period. The labels on the goods are your labels. We do not need them reprinted. We do need them to match the listing you give us afterwards.

The fee for being there is published: £780 ex VAT per site, per day, as a starting figure, then fixed in the engagement letter. It sits on top of the company statutory audit fee, which starts at £6,500 ex VAT where turnover is up to £15 million. You are not charged a separate fee for every line we test on the day. If the count needs a second day, or a second site, that is another day's attendance at the same published rate, agreed before we travel. Payment of the wider engagement is 40 percent at planning and 60 percent when the partner signs. VAT is extra on every invoice, and we bill in pounds sterling.

After the count, the listing has to agree to what was counted. That work sits in fieldwork, in weeks 4 to 9, once the records are with us. Records that arrive by week 4 are what allows a partner to sign within 12 weeks of the year-end. Priya Raman, the audit manager, will say at planning which documents the list contains. Expect the stock listing, the invoices behind our samples, and draft accounts before the findings meeting. Do not expect a request for every paper in the building.

The findings meeting is where you see what the count changed. Adjustments we propose are discussed there, with the partner in the room. The management letter then records what the directors should do differently next year: how the sheets are controlled, who can stop the warehouse, and how damaged or obsolete goods are identified. We do not publish a variance for Fenwick Joinery Ltd, the family joiner whose first audit turned on a timber count, and we will not invent one for you. The outcome of a count is a listing the partner can stand behind, or a clear statement that they cannot.

A planning call is the right place to test whether this year is that kind of year. It lasts 30 minutes and it is free, and we reply within 2 working days. Tell us how many places the stock lives, and send the latest accounts if you have them. If stock is not material, we will say so, and we will not sell you a day in the warehouse for the look of it. If it is material, we will be there, and a partner will sign the opinion afterwards. That signature is personal. It is not left to the senior who held the tally counter.

posts.title: What the management letter is for
posts.excerpt: The letter goes out with the partner’s signature: what we found, what was adjusted and what to change before the next year-end.
posts.content: The management letter is the working record of the audit. It lists what we found, what was adjusted and what we ask you to change. It makes no promise about the next opinion.
